newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Chechnya said close to signing peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Chechnya said close to signing peace deal.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov may sign an accord on a political settlement next week in Moscow, Interfax news agency said on Friday, quoting Maskhadov's spokesman.
The spokesman, Kazbek Khadzhiyev, said one point in the accord, aimed at turning a ceasefire between Russia and Chechnya into lasting peace, had not been agreed yet.
The two leaders were expected to iron out the differences during face-to-face talks due to take place between May 5 and 10, he said.
Khadzhiyev also said Yeltsin and Maskhadov were likely to sign a deal on economic issues.
A Russian presidential spokesman said he could not confirm the report but said such a meeting was "quite possible".
Russia and Chechnya agreed a ceasefire last summer after 21 months of war in which tens of thousands were killed, but talks have stalled on a political and economic settlement.

Maskhadov has been insisting on full independence. Moscow will not grant that and is offering what it calls broad sovereignity inside Russia. It is holding back funds to rebuild the Chechen economy until a final peace accord is signed.

The situation in the region deteriorated badly over the past week after a spate of violence in the districts neighbouring Chechnya, including fatal bomb attacks and the murder of an official in which some Russian officials saw "a Chechen link".

It appeared that the agreement about Maskhadov's visit to Moscow came during talks between Russian security officials and Chechen bosses held hastily in the Chechen capital Grozny on Wednesday and aimed at easing tension in the North Caucasus.

Movladi Udugov, deputy prime minister of Chechnya, who has held most of the talks with Russian officials, told Interfax the two delegations had done all they could and the fate of the accord was now in the hands of Maskhadov and Yeltsin.
"We are unable to make any steps further without the two presidents because neither side has corresponding powers," Udugov said.
